habitat: Green vine snakes, also known as long-nosed whip snakes, inhabit tropical forests, scrublands, and gardens across South and Southeast Asia, from India and Sri Lanka through Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia, and Indonesia. They are among the most arboreal of all snakes, spending virtually their entire lives in trees and dense vegetation. Their habitat preference includes secondary forests, agricultural edges, gardens, and plantations — they have adapted well to human-modified landscapes. They require dense foliage for both hunting and concealment from predators.
diet: Green vine snakes are specialized hunters of lizards, frogs, small birds, and occasionally small rodents. They are diurnal, using their binocular vision — a remarkable adaptation where each eye moves independently, giving them depth perception to strike prey from a distance. Their venom is mild and delivered through rear fangs; it is effective against small prey but not dangerous to humans (causing only mild swelling and numbness). They hunt by remaining motionless among foliage, swaying gently to mimic a vine blowing in the wind, then striking with lightning speed.
behavior: Green vine snakes are nervous, alert snakes that rely on camouflage and stillness as their primary defense. When threatened, they freeze, point their elongated snout upward, and sway slightly — becoming nearly invisible among foliage. If provoked further, they open their mouth to reveal a startling blue-black interior as a warning display. They are solitary animals that may tolerate others in areas with abundant prey. Females lay 3-12 elongated eggs among leaf litter or rotting wood. They are diurnal and can often be seen basking on branches in morning and late afternoon.
facts: The green vine snake's most distinctive feature is its extraordinary elongated snout, which gives it a comically pointed face and excellent binocular vision for judging distances to prey. They can flatten their body laterally to glide short distances between branches — one of the few snakes capable of limited aerial movement. Their body is pencil-thin, rarely exceeding 2 centimeters in diameter despite reaching 1.5-2 meters in length. They are mildly venomous but pose no significant threat to humans. Their green coloration provides near-perfect camouflage among leaves.
naming: Green vine snake names might reflect their vine-like appearance, green color, or serpentine grace. Consider names like Vine, Slinky, Whisper, Jade, Limon, Slender, Twig, Emerald, Reed, Sprout, Needle, Wisp, Sway, Viridis (green in Latin), or Chloros (green in Greek).
